issues.item: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: Given the trauma type is 'Police' and the patient is a 39-year-old female train conductor, this appraisal is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other items center on guilt about not preventing the event and persistent danger/startle responses, but 'failed in my most important role in life' implies a salient caregiving or identity-defining role that is not otherwise represented anywhere in the self-report. With no supporting memory, trigger, threat, or strategy content clarifying that role, this item stands out as clinically incoherent within the profile.

For a police trauma profile, the paired appraisals 'I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened' and 'I should have protected others and I failed' imply a specific moral-injury/responsibility theme in which the patient perceives herself as having failed to act or protect. That is coherent on its own, but it sits awkwardly with the trauma type label 'Police' for a 39-year-old female train conductor unless the trauma involved witnessing police harm to others in a context where she had a realistic protector role. This is not impossible, but it is the main item set that raises a clinical plausibility question relative to the indexed trauma context.

'Cannot Trust Safety' suggests a persistent current-threat belief that safety information from others is not believable. With no active edges in the formulation, each node is meant to be relatively isolated; however this threat item reads like a broad, generalized ongoing threat belief that would usually be mirrored by linked trigger, memory, appraisal, or strategy content. The rest of the profile instead centers on grief, sensory reliving, and guilt about failing to protect others. The combination is possible, but this particular threat item is the least well aligned with the otherwise responsibility/grief-focused profile and with a fully disconnected formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed
issues.explanation: For a civilian trauma type of police-related trauma, 'I should have protected others and I failed' implies a protector/responder role that is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile and demographics (train conductor, not police). The other selected items fit a victim/survivor stance (institutional failure, inability to trust safety, grief, sensory snapshot memory), so this specific appraisal stands out as clinically implausible for the same trauma narrative.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: 'Hypervigilance' is not a negative appraisal but a threat-monitoring/state-of-current-danger item. Its inclusion in the Negative Appraisals node is inconsistent with the cognitive formulation, especially because all inter-node edges are inactive and nodes should stand on their own rather than borrowing content from another component. The remaining appraisal items (institutional failure, self-blame) are coherent for police-related trauma, but this item is misplaced.

issues.item: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Within Negative Appraisals, these two items pull in opposing directions for the same police-related trauma: one locates primary responsibility in the self, while the other locates the core wrong in betrayal by a trusted other. These can sometimes coexist, but as the only appraisal items alongside institutional failure, the profile becomes hard to reconcile as a coherent single appraisal pattern for this trauma.

issues.item: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: For a police-related trauma, 'betrayal by someone I trusted' implies an interpersonal betrayal component that is not supported by the rest of the profile. The other appraisals center on institutional failure and injustice, which fit police trauma, but this item specifically suggests a trusted close other or ally personally betrayed the patient. With no corresponding memory, threat, trigger, or strategy content indicating an interpersonal betrayal trauma, this item is the least clinically coherent in the profile.
